title: A complete auroral oval is not a ground observation
bigIdea: An observation can support a global claim only when the viewpoint and sampling match the claim. A ground observer sees a local slice; a spacecraft can reveal the full oval.
prompt: What does the full oval let you claim that a ground observer cannot — and what would still require another measurement?
evidenceMove: Compare the full-oval ultraviolet view with a ground-view aurora photograph. Annotate direct observations, inferences and the parts of the system that remain unsampled.
extension: If the oval changes over 45 hours but you sample one location for 10 minutes, which features could you miss?

sources.label: NASA APOD — A Complete Auroral Oval from SMILE
ESA — SMILE’s first ultraviolet footage

title: The longer exposure changed the galaxy
bigIdea: New evidence does more than make an old picture clearer. A longer exposure reveals faint structure around M104, giving students a reason to revise a model of the galaxy’s history.
prompt: When the longer exposure reveals a halo and tidal streams, which part of your original model must change?
evidenceMove: Pair the short-exposure and deep image. Record what becomes visible, what is inferred from it, and how the proposed collision-and-merger history changes.
extension: What additional observation would help distinguish a merger history from another explanation for the faint structures?

sources.label: NASA APOD — M104: The Sombrero Galaxy’s Tidal Streams
NASA Webb — Sombrero Galaxy NIRCam image

title: One CTD profile is not the Pacific Ocean
bigIdea: A CTD cast can reveal temperature and salinity structure at one place and time. It cannot, by itself, establish the state of an entire ocean system.
prompt: What can this one temperature–salinity–depth profile tell you — and what can it not tell you about the Pacific?
evidenceMove: Plot temperature and salinity against depth. Mark claims supported by this cast, then list the extra spatial, temporal or repeat measurements needed for broader claims.
extension: What sampling plan would distinguish a local feature from a regional Pacific pattern?

sources.label: NOAA NCEI — Equatorial Pacific TAO CTD dataset
NOAA PSL — Vertical profile plots

title: Successful task completion is not yet validated learning
bigIdea: AI can improve engagement, confidence, task completion and the quality of a product without proving that the student can perform the underlying thinking independently.
prompt: If AI helps you complete a task successfully, what evidence would show that you can perform the underlying thinking without it?
evidenceMove: Compare an AI-assisted product with a cold response, an explanation of decisions and a transfer task. Classify which pieces show task completion and which show capability.
extension: Which forms of assistance make learning more likely rather than merely producing a better answer?

sources.label: University of Sydney — GenAI and school learning review
Barker Institute — Young people, learning and generative AI

title: Observe the satellite image before naming the place
bigIdea: Remote-sensing images become better evidence when students separate what is visible from what they infer. Identification is a conclusion, not the first observation.
prompt: What can you observe in this image before you name the place?
evidenceMove: Use three observations → two inferences → one question. Then inspect the image metadata or spectral bands and compare the evidence with the first guess.
extension: What extra band, time point or ground measurement would reduce your uncertainty most?

sources.label: NASA Earth Observatory — September 2026 Satellite Puzzler

title: One satellite snapshot is not a season
bigIdea: A single image can show simultaneous systems, but a causal or seasonal claim needs a time series, comparison data and a model of the relevant Earth system.
prompt: What does one satellite image show about the storms — and what would you need before claiming something about the season?
evidenceMove: Annotate direct evidence in the image, then compare it with the acquisition time, storm records and seasonal context. Keep the image separate from the explanation built around it.
extension: How could ocean temperature, wind shear and additional images test your explanation?

sources.label: NASA Earth Observatory — A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific

title: A new feature may be a new phenomenon — or a new view
bigIdea: A single surprising image cannot tell us whether a feature is new, newly visible or newly recognisable. Longitudinal observations and known gaps in coverage matter.
prompt: How can scientists tell whether Saturn’s decagon is new, newly visible, or simply newly recognisable?
evidenceMove: Compare older Cassini and Hubble images with the recent Hubble sequence. Mark observation gaps, changes in viewpoint and changes in the feature itself before making a claim.
extension: What additional observation would best distinguish a newly formed atmospheric wave from a feature that was previously hidden?

sources.label: ESA — Hubble tracks new decagon encircling Saturn’s south pole

title: One photograph can contain three different physical systems
bigIdea: An image may combine the object being studied, the intervening atmosphere and the geometry of the viewpoint. Not every visible feature belongs to the same system.
prompt: Which observations in this photograph tell us about the object itself, and which are consequences of viewing geometry or the atmosphere?
evidenceMove: Annotate the erupting volcano, the Moon and the Belt of Venus separately. Classify each claim as a direct observation, an inference or an explanation involving another system.
extension: What would change if the same scene were photographed from a different location, altitude or time?

sources.label: NASA APOD — Harvest Moon with Belt of Venus and Erupting Mount Etna

title: Zero recovered tags is still evidence
bigIdea: A null result does not automatically mean an experiment failed. Zero detections can be consistent with several explanations and can redirect the next measurement.
prompt: What can scientists legitimately conclude when 14,000 tagged moths produce zero recovered tags?
evidenceMove: Generate at least three explanations consistent with zero detections, then compare what each explanation predicts about population size, route, tag recovery and detection probability.
extension: How could citizen-science observations, extra traps or weather data distinguish among the explanations?

sources.label: ABC News — Scientists optimistic despite losing 14,000 tagged bogong moths

title: An autonomous vessel can measure — but can it do science?
bigIdea: Automation can extend measurement into places and seasons that are difficult for people to reach, but measurement, question-setting, validation and explanation remain different jobs.
prompt: An autonomous vessel collects Southern Ocean data for months at a time. Is it doing science?
evidenceMove: Separate the work into what the vessel does—navigate, measure, record and sample—and what scientists do—formulate questions, validate instruments, analyse evidence and evaluate explanations.
extension: Which part of the mission would be most vulnerable to an unnoticed sensor bias or missing data?

sources.label: CSIRO — Ocean drones set to brave the Southern Ocean for science

title: One voyage, four sciences, one evidence problem
bigIdea: Real investigations do not keep Biology, Chemistry, Physics and Earth Science in separate boxes. Different disciplines can ask complementary questions of the same place and evidence.
prompt: A research vessel reaches a seamount. What would a biologist, chemist, physicist and geologist each want to measure—and which question needs more than one discipline?
evidenceMove: Design one measurement or question for each discipline, then draw the evidence links needed to explain a shared phenomenon such as a seamount, shipwreck or microplastic distribution.
extension: What should the team do when two measurements appear to support different explanations?

sources.label: CSIRO — First international CAPSTAN voyage takes students to the Pacific

title: AI found the pattern — did AI discover it?
bigIdea: Pattern detection, interpretation, validation and a scientific claim are different stages. A model can accelerate the first stage without completing the others.
prompt: If an AI identifies a new lunar feature in decades of images, what evidence is needed before it becomes a scientific discovery?
evidenceMove: Map the chain from detection to interpretation to independent validation to published claim. Ask what could create false positives at each step.
extension: How could a second dataset, instrument or research team test the proposed feature?

sources.label: NASA — NASA, IBM Launch AI Foundation Model for Lunar Science
IBM — NASA–IBM Lunar Foundation Model

title: Processing can reveal evidence without becoming the evidence
bigIdea: Calibration, stacking and artifact removal can make observations more useful, but the processing history remains part of the evidence that others need to evaluate.
prompt: When does processing clarify an observation, and when might it make the evidence harder to trust?
evidenceMove: Compare the raw and processed Andromeda images. Identify artifacts, legitimate corrections and transformations that should be disclosed so another observer can reproduce the result.
extension: What changes if two teams process the same data with different pipelines?

sources.label: NASA APOD — Andromeda Before Photoshop

title: One rock can hold more than one history
bigIdea: New evidence can complicate an explanation rather than simply replace it. A rock can preserve evidence of several environments and episodes through time.
prompt: How should a model of Jezero’s history change when the same rock records several episodes of water alteration?
evidenceMove: Build an initial lake-based explanation from orbital evidence, then add rover measurements showing groundwater, lake and later heated-water interactions. Revise the timeline rather than discarding every earlier clue.
extension: What additional measurement would best constrain the order or age of the water events?

sources.label: NASA — Complex water systems on early Mars

title: An anomaly is evidence to investigate, not proof of a leak
bigIdea: Automated pattern detection can flag an unusual observation at scale, but the anomaly still needs interpretation and independent verification before it becomes a conclusion.
prompt: A school meter records 350 L per hour between 1:00 am and 4:00 am for five nights. What can you infer—and what can you not conclude yet?
evidenceMove: Separate the meter observation, plausible explanations and verification steps. Ask students to identify false positives such as cleaning, irrigation, faulty meters or unusual building use.
extension: What extra sensor, comparison period or controlled test would reduce uncertainty most?

sources.label: NSW Water — New AI leak detection technology

title: Invisible does not mean unmeasurable
bigIdea: Scientists can map entities they cannot see directly by measuring how those entities alter something observable. The evidence is indirect but still testable.
prompt: How can scientists map a magnetic field that nobody can see?
evidenceMove: Use the idea that the polarisation of light twists as it travels through a magnetic field. Distinguish direct observation of galaxies from inference about the intervening field.
extension: What assumptions, calibration steps or independent observations would make the inferred map more convincing?

sources.label: CSIRO — Most detailed map of the Universe’s hidden magnetic fields

title: A PISA headline is not an education diagnosis
bigIdea: A headline compresses several measures into a claim. Students need to inspect what was measured, how it was compared and what conclusion the data can support.
prompt: Can a claim about Australia’s ‘worst-ever’ reading scores tell you that Australian students are worse at learning?
evidenceMove: Separate the measure, sample, comparison group, uncertainty and interpretation. Compare subject scores with the separate PISA digital-world measures before accepting a broad conclusion.
extension: What additional evidence would distinguish changes in reading performance from changes in what the assessment measures?

sources.label: OECD — PISA 2025 Results: Australia
OECD — PISA 2025 Learning in the Digital World

title: A legitimate goal does not make every method legitimate
bigIdea: An agent can turn a legitimate objective into unanticipated actions. Evaluating an AI system therefore requires checking goals, constraints, tool access, logs and outcomes.
prompt: If an AI is given a legitimate goal, is every method it chooses to achieve that goal legitimate?
evidenceMove: Separate the instruction, goal, chosen action and violated constraint. Ask students to design a guardrail and an audit trail that would make the behaviour detectable.
extension: Which matters more for trust: a successful outcome, a compliant method, or evidence that the system stayed within its constraints?

sources.label: Australian Government PM&C — Rapid review into an AI-driven cyber incident

title: Seasons can look different from the wrong viewpoint
bigIdea: A stable three-dimensional system can appear to change in a surprising way when viewed from a distant position. Predictions help separate geometry from physical change.
prompt: If Earth’s orbit causes the seasons, what should change in full-Earth images between the solstices and equinoxes?
evidenceMove: Predict the apparent movement of continents and seasonal surface features, then compare those predictions with the DSCOVR EPIC image sequence and explain the role of axial tilt.
extension: What could you estimate about Earth’s axial tilt from a longer sequence of full-disk images?

sources.label: NASA Earth Observatory — An Epic View of the Seasons

title: Before the printer, engineer the powder
bigIdea: A machine’s performance depends on the material it processes. Particle size, shape and flow can matter before the printer settings are adjusted.
prompt: What does a metal 3D printer need besides a design, a machine and heat?
evidenceMove: Compare possible metal feedstocks—filings, dust, cubes and spheres—and predict how particle properties might affect flow, melting, defects and final strength.
extension: Which material property would you measure first if a printed part repeatedly developed weak layers?

sources.label: CSIRO — From powder to possibility

title: A faster computer can change the questions
bigIdea: A thousand-fold increase in computation does more than shorten old calculations. It can make new datasets, models and scientific questions possible.
prompt: When a calculation becomes 1,000 times faster, what new science might become possible?
evidenceMove: Estimate the new time for a 20-minute calculation, then compare ‘doing the same calculation faster’ with ‘asking a question that was previously impractical’.
extension: Which modern scientific questions would still be impossible if computation stopped improving?

sources.label: CSIRO — Building Australia’s first computer
